fact_text
Your gut hosts roughly as many microbial cells as you have human ones — you are, charitably, half you.
People who eat 30 or more different plants a week host measurably more diverse gut microbes than people who eat 10, no matter how "healthy" those 10 are.
Your microbes make most of your body's serotonin down in the gut — the plants you feed them are part of that supply chain.
Fibre isn't one thing — there are dozens of types, and different microbes specialise in different ones. Variety literally feeds a wider crew.
Garlic's inulin survives cooking — roasted whole heads are still a feast for your fibre-fermenting crews.
Onions keep most of their quercetin in the outer layers — peel gently and you keep the good part.
A leek's white base is where the fructans hide — the part people trim off is the prebiotic part.
Cooking tomatoes doesn't destroy lycopene — it concentrates it. Sauce is a feature, not a compromise.
Cooled potatoes grow resistant starch as they chill — potato salad genuinely feeds different microbes than hot mash.
The same trick works with rice: cook it, cool it overnight, and some starch re-crystallises into microbe food.
A green banana and a ripe banana are almost different foods to your gut — the greener one carries far more resistant starch.
Chewing broccoli is what activates its most-studied compound — the enzyme only meets its target when you break the cells.
Kale, cabbage, and Brussels sprouts are all the same species — Brassica oleracea, bred into wildly different shapes.
Beetroot's colour is betalain, and it's doing more than staining your fingers — that pigment is the point.
Half an avocado has more fibre than two slices of wholemeal bread — a fruit that eats like a fat.
Raspberries carry around eight grams of fibre per cup — one of the highest of any fruit you can buy.
Pomegranate feeds a compound called urolithin A that only certain people's microbes can make — eat it and find out if you're one.
The ellagitannins in walnuts get converted by gut bacteria into the same urolithins as pomegranate — nuts and fruit, same pathway.
Oats owe their reputation to beta-glucan, a soluble fibre your microbes ferment into compounds that talk to the rest of your body.
Chicory root is where most supplement-bottle inulin actually comes from — the plant version is the original.
Jerusalem artichokes are so rich in inulin they're nicknamed "fartichokes" — start with a small amount and let your microbes adjust.
Turmeric's curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own, but a crack of black pepper can help it along.
Herbs punch far above their weight — oregano and thyme carry some of the densest polyphenol loads in the kitchen.
A handful of fresh herbs counts as a plant toward your 30 — parsley isn't just a garnish.
Fermented foods can carry billions of live microbes per serving — kimchi and kefir are crews you can eat.
Miso goes in after the heat is off — boiling water kills the very cultures you added it for.
Real sourdough is fermented dough — the long rise is bacteria and wild yeast pre-digesting the flour for you.
Flaxseeds pass straight through you whole — grind them first, or their lignans stay locked inside.
Chia's magic is mucilage, the gel it forms in water — a soluble fibre your butyrate-makers love.
Berries get their deep blues and purples from anthocyanins, the same pigments that feed your gut's barrier-guarding crews.
Eating an orange beats drinking it — the fibre and much of the hesperidin live in the segments and pith.
Mushrooms aren't plants, but their beta-glucans still count toward the diversity your microbes crave.
Seaweed carries fibres — like fucoidan — that simply don't exist in land plants. A different feed entirely.
Lentils cook in 25 minutes with no soaking and deliver GOS, one of the top bacterial fuels going.
The skin is where a lot of the action is — apples, grapes, and aubergines keep their best compounds just under the peel.
